strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: learning conversational preferences from naturally occurring user feedback. The construction of 20,281 preference examples from real multi-turn conversations is a potentially useful resource contribution.

The GPT-4-generated dataset yields consistent improvements across three model families and three standard benchmarks. For example, Phi 3 improves from 24.3% to 34.9% on AlpacaEval 2 length-controlled win rate and from 15.4% to 32.4% on Arena-Hard. These results provide meaningful evidence of training utility beyond the proposed evaluation.

The feedback detector receives human validation using four experts, 50 conversations, and adjudicated annotations. Reporting precision, recall, and both human–human and model–human agreement makes the detector’s limitations assessable.

The pipeline is understandable, with detailed annotation/evaluation prompts and core training hyperparameters. The reported separation of training and test users and conversations is appropriate, and the checklist/no-checklist comparison usefully exposes evaluator sensitivity.
weaknesses: The central claim of improved alignment with actual users lacks independent validation. GPT-4o identifies feedback, summarizes preferences, generates expert preferred responses, and judges WildFeedback outputs using those summaries. Figure 2 therefore establishes sensitivity to the supplied checklist, rather than demonstrating that checklist-guided judgments agree better with users. Human annotation validates only SAT/DSAT detection, not summary faithfulness, generated preference pairs, or final response rankings. A blinded human evaluation grounded in the original feedback is needed to support the proposed evaluation’s validity.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of in-situ feedback. Comparisons are principally against the original instruction-tuned models; there is no matched GPT-4 regeneration baseline without feedback guidance, SFT-only ablation, or comparable training on an existing preference dataset. Furthermore, the GPT-4 and on-policy variants differ in dataset size, response sources, and filtering. Consequently, the improvements could substantially reflect teacher distillation or additional training rather than the proposed feedback mechanism.

The evaluation’s population-level interpretation is insufficiently supported. Selecting ten examples with mutually similar preferences from each of 70 clusters deliberately emphasizes central preferences and training-related tasks. This can serve a restricted evaluation objective, but does not establish representativeness of the broader user population or even population-weighted majority preferences. The detector’s 48.4% DSAT recall on the validation sample introduces additional coverage concerns. A randomly sampled held-out evaluation and analysis by feedback type would help establish the scope of the findings.

The claim that training on either dataset version does not compromise other benchmark performance is contradicted by Table 3. On-policy Mistral drops from 17.1% to 12.9% on AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate, 12.6% to 10.3% on Arena-Hard, and 6.71 to 6.42 on MT-Bench. The discussion should acknowledge this tradeoff. Repeated claims of significant or robust improvements also lack uncertainty estimates, particularly relevant to the small MT-Bench differences.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendices. The dataset is only promised for future release, with no linked code or split artifacts. Important details remain unspecified, including the clustering embedding model, precise filtering rules, data-generation decoding settings, hyperparameter selection criterion, and whether preference system prompts are retained during SFT/DPO. These omissions affect reconstruction of both the training data and the custom evaluation.

Claims of overcoming model bias and subjectivity, capturing 'true human values,' and supporting real-time adaptation exceed the evidence from an offline, heavily model-mediated pipeline. The promising benchmark results support a narrower contribution, but the missing controlled comparisons and independent preference validation are substantive revisions that warrant resubmission next cycle.
